utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Can we have the accused brought in, please? (The accused was brought in).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Prosecution, we can now continue the statement of your witness, Mr. Djidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, if Mr. Djidic could be brought up to the courtroom. MR. DJIDIC (cont'd) Examination-in-chief by MR. KEHOE (cont'd):

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. Djidic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, when we broke on Friday we were talking about the establishment of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosnia in late 1991. After the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosnia came into existence did life for the Muslims in the Lasva Valley and in the Vitez area become more difficult?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Life for the Muslims became more and more difficult by the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber how?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, the authorities of Herceg-Bosnia formed the authority of the HVO, which was a one nation authority, and in time and to be more precise in May 1992, all Muslims were expelled from the bodies of authority. At that time, we had a joint parliament. We had a joint government. The Croats were in the majority and they controlled fully all authority. And knowing that, that they were fully in control, one may ask why did they chase the Muslims out of the bodies of government? That is the most important question, which shows that the Croats did not wish to have Muslims in the authorities. In the course of the spring of 1992, certain conditions started to be attached for the continued work of people within the bodies of authority. So that a separation occurred of the Muslims from the executive authorities. It is particularly worth noting that at that time the Croats offered to the Muslims a certain piece of paper which they had to sign, recognising the authorities of Herceg-Bosnia. All those who did not wish to do so could no longer continue working. In June an attack occurred against the police station, and on that occasion policemen of Muslim faith were disarmed and thrown out of the police station. This attack on the police station was carried out by members of the HOS headed by Darko Kraljevic. After that date the Muslims never again returned to that station. Muslims then went to Stari Vitez and a few days later they formed a separate police station. That police station is operated in Stari Vitez to this day. At the time, that is in June and after June, the Muslims continued to be terrorised. The people were intimidated. Muslim owned hotels and restaurants were blown up. Then the Muslims' flats were broken into, with demands being made for them to give up weapons, and also money. The Muslims were taken away for so-called informative interviews, after which they would come back with visible traces of mistreatment. It is particularly worth noting that the HVO at that time, and throughout 1992, was also settling accounts with disobedient -- disobedient Croats and Serbs. Individuals were taken into custody for informative interviews. I do not know whether they were mistreated. Also, at about the same time, there were frequent attempts, many were successful, to restore peace to Vitez and there were endless meetings with the Croats, and, at times, some success was achieved. But the police has never worked together since, nor did the Muslims rejoin the parliament, or the government. Various kinds of provocations continued, which frequently resulted in the arrests of Muslims, both civilians and members of the army. More and more people were being laid off. And roughly about that time the HVO introduced a new currency. We would be given our salaries in Croatian dinars, which is the currency of the neighbouring state of Croatia. The Muslims had to accept this, because they had no other currency, or rather the Bosnian dinar, at that time, was undergoing spiralling inflation and could not be used in the so-called Herceg-Bosnia. All attempts made to restore confidence for people to be able to live and work normally failed, and this went on like this throughout the year 1992, and at the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, going back to some of the statements that you just made concerning the legislature. You said that there was a greater percentage of Croats than there were Muslims. Approximately what was the ratio of Croats to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In relation to the Muslims in Vitez there were only 3 or 4 per cent more Croats than Muslims. As for the figure itself, in nominal terms this means about 1,000 Croats more. The municipality of Vitez at that time had about 26,000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned, Mr. Djidic, the HVO. What is the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO is the Croatian Defence Council, which consisted of civilians, and of a civilian and military part. Both the civilian and the military authorities were referred to as the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within the HVO was the civilian and the military side very close?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the HVO came into existence did the legislature that you talked about continue to sit and discuss matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The parliament or legislature continued to exist, but for a very short time. I do not remember exactly when it ceased to exist as a joint body, because I was not a member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, were there particular political leaders in Vitez which in your opinion attempted to divide the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, and if so who are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were. At that time the most prominent among them were people who, in the municipal authority and who headed the HDZ party. Those were Mr. Ivica Santic who was the town mayor of Vitez at the time, then Pero Skopljak and Anto Valenta who was then President of the HDZ. Those were the key figures who worked to establish the authority of the HVO, or the so-called Croatian community of Herceg-Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, let us talk about these individuals one by one starting with Anto Valenta. Did you know Anto Valenta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He worked as an engineer, a chemistry engineer in the military facility. While I was working in a school, Anto Valenta taught chemistry as a teacher. He was a friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Anto Valenta publish a book of the ethnic division of the Lasva Valley and other areas in central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain that to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anto Valenta was the first to write a book with maps of the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina along ethnic lines, that is he envisaged ethnically pure areas. That book was published, and it is not difficult to come by it. It was published even before the elections in the '80s; and I think that much was taken from Anto Valenta's book for the establishment and the achievement of the division of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Anto Valenta have a particular role within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Anto Valenta was first the President of the HDZ, Croatian democratic community, and after some time he was appointed Deputy President of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosnia, the deputy of Mr. Boban, therefore he was a very high ranking Croatian official.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about Ivica Santic, what can you tell the court about Ivica Santic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Ivica Santic very well indeed as well. He is also a chemistry engineer. He specialises in plastic materials. He was my teacher in secondary school. He taught chemistry, and we worked together in the factory. The house he was born in is only 1 kilometre away from mine, and our parents knew each other too. At the time, he was the town mayor in the Vitez municipality. We were friends as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the tensions in the Lasva Valley began to rise in 1992 what was the position of Ivica Santic concerning the rights of the Bosnian Croats and the HVO as opposed to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivica Santic was town mayor, as I have said. All important decisions were taken by the mayor. In any event, he was very much in control. The Muslims were not a hindrance to him. However, the policies of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosnia had different objectives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to the third individual you talked about Pero Skopljak. Can you tell the court about Pero Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Pero Skopljak, after the elections in 1991, was appointed head of the police in Vitez, of the SUP, which is the present Ministry of Internal Affairs. He worked there for a time, and then he went to work as the President of the HDZ. I did not know him as well as Santic and Valenta. I know that he graduated in theology at the university, so he was a priest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the individual named Mario Cerkez, do you know Mario Cerkez and if you do can you tell the court about Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know Mario Cerkez very well. We worked together in the same factory. First we were colleagues in the same service and later on I was his superior. This was a young man who was very polite, disciplined. He liked to work. And his assignment in the service was to take care of material and technical resources, and of the weapons that we used in defence of the factory. We would visit each other for holidays, and when new comers joined us, or rather when we had -- when children were born we would exchange visits. He visited my house several times, as I did his.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving outside the Vitez area do you know an individual named Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did not know Dario Kordic until 1991. I met him as the leader of the Bosnian Croats. I think he was President of the HDZ in Busovaca and after some time he also became a very high ranking official in Herceg-Bosnia. Also I would see him frequently wearing a uniform. He had some military assignments and duties as well. I do not know much about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the accused Tihomir Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met Tihomir Blaskic in 1992 when he came to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him prior to that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role did the accused, Blaskic, have in Vitez when he came in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When Blaskic came to Vitez he came as commander of the operational zone of central Bosnia. At that time, the commander of the operative zone, or rather the headquarters of that zone, was actually being established at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw Blaskic in the Vitez area was he normally dressed in a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe that uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Blaskic frequently wore a black uniform, and he also were a camouflage uniform. When we were officially introduced it was at the stadium in Vitez when the HVO was taking an oath. That was when I met Blaskic. And at that time he was wearing a black uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just explain that oath taking ceremony a little bit more. Explain this oath taking ceremony. Was there an oath taking ceremony by the army of Bosnia and then by the HVO? Could you explain that to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. First of all members of the TO gave an oath, and that happened before the school where the headquarters was situated. I invited every one. The military and political authorities of the HVO were to be present there as guests to witness the oaths. A great number of Croats accepted the invitation and were present at the ceremony. A month or a month and a half later, HVO also gave an oath at the City stadium in Vitez. They also invited Muslims to be present as guests. I was one of the guests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who spoke at this oath taking ceremony for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the mayor spoke, the mayor Santic spoke, then Mario Cerkez and Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they say? What did they talk about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The speeches made by these people mainly concentrated on saying that it was the duty of the Croats to defend Croatian areas, the so-called Herceg-Bosnia, with the aim of defending spaces which historically belonged to Croatia. And these areas were in fact areas which belonged to both sides. It was specially Dario Kordic who called upon Croats to fight to the last man for these areas, for this territory. He also sent a message to Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, then President of the State, that soldiers of the HVO shall fight for Herceg-Bosnia with their bodies and souls. He was applauded and given an ovation, a military style ovation and it is especially noteworthy that they gave him a fascist style salute, ready for the motherland. That was the salute of the Ustasha from the second world war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the speech by Dario Kordic make you uncomfortable, and if so why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did. Dario Kordic's speech was specially unpleasant to me, very unpleasant. I was sorry to be there at all. I was sorry to be listening to those things. If anybody had told me beforehand I would not have believed them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, what about that speech would you not have believed? Explain to the court. What got your attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not have believed that there could be anyone in this world who could dislike coexistence between nations in Bosnia, and who wanted that state only for themselves, for one nation. Nor could I believe that Croats could be so much bothered by Muslims, because there had not been a single gesture to show that in that so-called Herceg-Bosnia other nations were living as well, besides the Croats, such as Muslims, Serbs, members of other nationalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Blaskic there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was he seated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Blaskic was up there with the guests at the elevated stands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you referring to a podium?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it could be called that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, you said that Blaskic dressed in black.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the dressing in black indicate to the Muslims, or to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It meant nothing to me personally. In my view, anybody is free to wear whatever they please. However, a black uniform is traditionally the uniform worn by the Ustasha in the Second World War. This is not to say that Mr. Blaskic is an Ustasha. There were also Muslims who wore black uniforms. Everybody had their own reasons for choosing a black uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, is the individual you are referring to as Mr. Blaskic, Tihomir Blaskic, is he in the courtroom here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Point to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the man (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time if we could hand out what has been marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 80, with the assistance of the usher. (Handed). Mr. President, if I could ask the court's indulgence and ask for the usher to stand with Mr. Djidic and take this particular exhibit apart and put the photographs on the ELMO it might be a little more easier as Mr. Djidic is not as experienced with the use of the ELMO as the usher is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that would be fine Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have marked a series of exhibits as Prosecutor's Exhibit 80. If we could take that apart Mr. Usher and go photograph by photograph. It might be easier on the ELMO if we just take it apart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This document which is 80, is this in fact the photograph which is on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is a composite Exhibit 80. In the lower right-hand corner there is a number 22-446. That will be the photograph on the ELMO right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, turn if you can with the pointer and with the individual photograph that is on the ELMO; do you recognise these two individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This man here (Indicates) is Mr. Blaskic. And this man here (Indicates) is Mr. Alagic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that particular photograph is the defendant Blaskic wearing a black uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to the next photograph, which is Z2447. Who are the individuals in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one is Mr. Blaskic (Indicates). This is Mr. Mahmuljin. This is Mr. Alagic, and this man I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way Mr. Djidic, General Alagic, who is General Alagic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Alagic was commander of the VII Corp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us draw our attention to the next photograph, sir. Who do you recognise in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates) This is Mr. Blaskic. Behind him (Indicates) the man in the white overcoat is a doctor from Vitez. I do not know anyone else here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That particular photograph, your Honour, that is on the ELMO right now, Z2448. Now, in that photograph, Mr. Djidic, Mr. Blaskic has a camouflage uniform on, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the existence of the usher, turn your attention to the next photograph which is Z2449. Can you just centre that a little bit? Do you recognise any of these people in Z2449?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This man here (Indicates) is Milvoy Petkovic. And Mr. Blaskic is the one behind him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is Milvoy Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milvoy Petkovic is a high ranking officer in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to the next photograph which is Z2450. Again, who are these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We see again Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Blaskic. I know this man here, but I cannot remember his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Keep going on, Mr. Djidic. We are talking about now Z2445. If we could put that next photograph on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this photograph I recognise Mr. Filip Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He is the individual on the right-hand side with the grey hair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Good.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Next to him sits Mr. Blaskic, and this man here (Indicates), is Franjo Nakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher could we move to the next photograph Z2456? Do you recognise any of these men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates) this is Mr. Kostroman from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is Mr. Kostroman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Kostroman is an official of the HDZ from Busovaca. I think it was him. It was he who organised the press conferences of the HVO for the television in Busovaca and Vitez. I do not know for sure what his duties were, but he appeared very often at those press conferences as the host.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else appeared at those press conferences besides Kostroman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This man here is Dario Kordic (Indicates). This one is Anto Valenta, and this civilian is from Vitez, I think his name is also Anto.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turn your attention to the next photograph, Z2457, if we could put that on the ELMO. Could you point out the individuals on that photograph that you recognise? If we could shift that a little bit to the right? Can we move that over just a little bit so we get the full photograph? A little bit more. Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Anto Valenta (Indicates). This is Pero Skopljak. This is Ivica Santic (Indicates). That man is the Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, are these the three individuals Anto Valenta, Ivica Santic and Pero Skopljak, who you described as being some of the political leaders of Herceg-Bosnia which gave such a difficult time to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those are the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to the next photograph, Z2458.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Mr. Blaskic (Indicates). This is Mr. Kordic (Indicates). Mr. Kulstrama (Indicates). I think this is Anto Spajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Staying with that photograph, Mr. Djidic, Z2457 you mentioned previously that Kostroman was one of the individuals at the press conference, and that Kordic was often there with him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the defendant Blaskic with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen Blaskic as well, but not many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When these individuals were on television what were they discussing at these press conferences?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can we have some clarification as to "these individuals".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The three individuals, Kostroman Kordic and Blaskic. When they were on television at these press conferences, Mr. Djidic, what were they talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, press conferences were held very often. They usually discussed decisions of the HVO government, decisions of the government of the HDZ, the Croatian democratic community; and the assignments given by these authorities. Also these press conferences discussed military operations which were then underway in Bosnia, carried out by the Serbian aggressor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it appear to you, Mr. Djidic, that these individuals were working together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to the final photograph in this exhibit, Z2459. If we could put that on the ELMO, with the assistance of the usher. Again, just point out the individuals you recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates) This here is Mr. Kulstrama. This is Mr. Kordic (Indicates). This is Anto Valenta (Indicates). And this is another Anto. I do not recognise the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecutor would offer into evidence Prosecutor's Exhibit 80. With the assistance of the usher if we could put that exhibit back together again, and we will move on with the questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson, with the agreement of both parties the whole album is going to be 80. Exhibit 80, is that correct? Actually, no, we are going to take a 10 minute break because we are going to finish at 5. We will suspend the hearing for 10 minutes. (4.00 pm) (Short Break). (4.20 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume our hearing, please be seated. Mr. Kehoe, proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Djidic, just to clarify a couple of points. During your testimony concerning the swearing in ceremony you noted there was a swearing in ceremony for the Territorial Defence. Could you explain to The Chamber what the Territorial Defence was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence implied the organisation of the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina intended to defend the whole territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the areas that were not swept by the war, that is wherever that was possible. Its aim was protection of all citizens living in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather in those parts where it was possible to organise it. The Territorial Defence consisted of people of all ethnic backgrounds, but the Muslims were the most numerous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, you were in the Territorial Defence in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it solely a Muslim function, or were there only Muslims in the Territorial Defence in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In the Territorial Defence of Vitez there were both Croats and Serbs and Muslims. In the TO headquarters there were officers who were Croats, who worked in the Territorial Defence for a period of time. Mostly all the officers of the former JNA, who were expelled or who had fled from the JNA, were involved in the Territorial Defence. With the formation of the HVO, a separation occurred among these people, too, that is officers of Croatian ethnic background left the duties they performed within the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they leave voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The officers abandoned the Territorial Defence headquarters, but there was a certain amount of pressure on the part of the HVO on individual officers and soldiers. There were some who left the TO headquarters with tears in their eyes, because some of them did not agree with the policies of the HDZ, and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just changing subjects a little bit Mr. Djidic, can you explain to the court what the crisis committee was in Vitez, when it was established, and what it was set up to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The crisis staff is a body formed with its main goal being to try to link the civilian with the military authorities, to tackle certain problems, and to focus on defence against the Chetniks. It was a group of people from the civilian and military authorities. It was of mixed composition, that is consisting of Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who was on the crisis staff, who was on the crisis committee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do remember quite a number of them. They were mostly political and military leaders. The people I have already mentioned: the mayor, the presidents of the parties, the general managers of large work organisations, businessmen, simply people who were able to make decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, are you saying that Mayor Santic was on that committee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pero Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pero Skopljak, Marjan Skopljak, Anto Valenta, Mario Cerkez. I was on it. Mr. Kaknjo, Mr. Kajmovic, Dr Mujezinovic and some others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the establishment of the HVO and -- did you attempt, through the crisis committee to have the HVO and the Territorial Defence work together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was not just me. At that time the division was still not so pronounced. There were agreements in principle that a joint brigade should be formed, which would consist of both Croats and Muslims. There were even proposals as to who would be in the command of that brigade, since the Croats were the majority population in Vitez. On one occasion we had agreed that the brigade commander should be a Croat, Mr. Nakic, and that his deputy should be a Muslim, and I was supposed to be that. We had a group of people, particularly officers, who had escaped from the former JNA whose assignment it was to prepare a plan for the establishment of such a joint brigade. People were enthusiastic about it. However, that joint brigade was never in effect established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any proposals on any side as to what this joint brigade was going to be named?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were various proposals made. But it was mostly expected to be a joint brigade, and its task would have been to defend Vitez. In the subsequent negotiations, the HDZ and the HVO did not agree to such a joint brigade, but demanded that there should be a joint brigade, but that it should be an HVO brigade. In other words, that the activities of the Territorial Defence in Vitez should be suspended, which was certainly not acceptable to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who in the HVO refused to go along with the joint brigades of Muslims and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly the political leaders. At a meeting once when we were discussing a joint unit and how we would call it, a friend of mine, a Croat who was sitting next to me at the meeting proposed, to me, that the insignia for the military could be HMVO, standing for the Croatian Muslim Defence Council, the majority of people were eager to accept such a proposal. We left the meeting in the conviction that we would succeed. However, in a couple of days Anto Valenta said that nothing would come of it, and then there were further attempts made to link the TO and the HVO, but we were not successful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Valenta tell you why nothing was going to come of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He made explanations at meetings about this. The policy of the HVO in Herceg-Bosnia was that there could be only one army, and that army would have to be the HVO. That the TO should be extinguished. Anto Valenta, in particular, referred to the example of Mostar and at that time in Mostar there was a large scale war going on, major attacks by the Chetnics and a large number of Muslims were in the HVO. And he would say that the Muslims of Vitez, too, should come under the control and the command of the HVO, which did not favour a solution that will be acceptable to all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now during what time frame are these negotiations and discussions taking place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These discussions were taking place in the course of 1992, and even into the beginning of 1993. First, there was talk of a joint army, then about the HVO alone, and then after the first clash talk was again revived about a joint army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us talk a little bit about this build up to the first clash. Can you describe that to the court? What was going on before the first clash, and then discuss with the court the actual first clash?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first clash between the army and the HVO in Vitez occurred on the 20th October, 1992. And on a broader area of central Bosnia, on the 18th of October, the HVO attacked Novi Travnik. The conflict went on for two or three days, and after that, approximately for a month, the HVO intensified its pressure on the TO, to place itself under the command of the HVO. A month later, the situation on the front changed. The Chetnics made advances on several fronts. And negotiations were under way regarding the new structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and people were waiting to see what would happen. In any event, around the month of October I received several ultimatums, to the effect that the Territorial Defence should surrender its weapons and place itself under the command of the HVO. The political situation led up to this actually not taking place. On one occasion, Mr. Blaskic, at a meeting when I went to him, said that no one had the right to force anyone to come under his command, which was correct on his part. Probably Mr. Blaskic, in those days, was better informed about the situation on the front than the HVO political leaders. And after the conflict, there was a period of attempts being made to organise a joint struggle against the Chetnics. And there were some very good proposals made to send -- deploy units on the front. Something changed within the HVO, and especially when, at the end of October, the Chetnics captured Jajce. The Chetnics captured Jajce immediately after the conflict in Vitez. And, as a sign of goodwill to co-operate and defend Bosnia, I proposed to Mr. Cerkez that we should jointly organise the Croats and the Muslims, and position them outside the hotel in Vitez, so that all the citizens of Vitez would see them, so that both Muslim mothers, and Croat mothers could weep as they despatched their sons to the front. My idea was to restore trust among the people, so that the people could feel more secure, because if they had seen Muslims and Croats jointly going to the front to fight the Chetnics, surely life in Vitez would have improved, and not only in Vitez but broader. My idea did not succeed. I did not manage to come to an agreement with Mario. In any case, at that time, it was Mr. Blaskic who took control, as well as Mr. Merdan who had highly productive meetings and agreements, first of all the army could move around without any difficulty, but the agreement was that a day in advance the departure of the army to the front should be announced. The exact number of men going, and the line of movement, where they would be going to. This had to be done so as to ease tensions, and so that there would be no obstacles in passing through checkpoints which existed at the time. But unfortunately only TO members in those days were going to fight the Chetnics. The front was at Visoko and the Vlasic, Mont Vlasic. Whereas HVO members took positions on the nearby hill above Vitez, called Kuber, and there were never any Chetnics there. It was only later that parts of units of the HVO joined in the struggle against the Chetnics, on the ground, in the area between Novi Travnik and Travnik, where very few HVO soldiers from Vitez, I am talking about soldiers from Vitez only, very few of them were on the confrontation line with the Chetnics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just going back, Mr. Djidic, you mentioned that the first conflict was in Novi Travnik in October. What was that conflict all about. Why was there a fight in Novi Travnik in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not in Novi Travnik at the time, but throughout central Bosnia-Herzegovina the problems were very much alike and those were that attempts were being made by the HVO for TO members to be placed under the HVO command, or rather for the Muslims to be disarmed. The situation in all the towns of central Bosnia was virtually identical. What were the real reasons? In Novi Travnik and how the conflict broke out I can only assume, but it is the same kind of policy of the HVO, that was implemented in Vitez as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the conflict in Novi Travnik, did you participate in a phone call with Froid Kaknjo to Dario Kordic to discuss this conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I listened to a telephone conversation between Kordic and Kaknjo. The two of them were talking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion, Mr. Kaknjo needed to call up Mr. Kordic, because there was a lot of shooting going on in Novi Travnik, and in those days we were having meetings in Vitez. He wanted to consult him over something. However, when he raised the receiver and asked for Kordic he did not hear his voice, because Mr. Kordic was apparently speaking on another line, on maybe on the Motorola, so he passed the receiver to me, and he said listen to Kordic, and I heard clearly that he was issuing orders, among other words I heard, I heard he was shouting at someone, and he said "burn that over there", I do not know what he had in mind, what he was referring to. Then a couple of minutes later Kordic took the receiver and said to Kaknjo, using rough words, unkind words, that he did not have any time for him. At that time, while the two of them were talking, Kordic was in Novi Travnik, and his number was known to Kaknjo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Novi Travnik was in the central Bosnia operative zone at that time, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the central Bosnia operative zone in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, Mr. Blaskic was the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The defendant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shortly after the outbreak in hostilities in Novi Travnik was there trouble in the Vitez area including the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain that to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Somewhere around the 18th October I was informed that the HVO had attacked Novi Travnik. In the afternoon I left home and at the checkpoint the HVO checkpoint at the railway station of Vitez, I saw a small column of vehicles, three or four trucks, with quite a large number of soldiers in them. In the first truck I saw Mr. Kordic. He was in uniform. He had a walkie-talkie attached to his lapel of his uniform and the HVO soldiers, who happened to be at the checkpoint, were saluting him, even a neighbour of mine called Ivo Vidovic took out a big knife and waved it as a sign of greeting. The HVO tried to stop me at that checkpoint, but I managed to pass in the direction of Vitez. The column in which Kordic was left along the transit road going along side Vitez to Novi Travnik. After that, I got in touch with the brigade commander, or rather of the Territorial Defence, at that time, in Novi Travnik, Mr. Lendo, who told me that the TO had been attacked. Also, I got in touch with Mr. Merdan and told him what I had heard, and he told me that he had been informed about it. I asked Mr. Lendo how I could be of assistance, and he said: "There is nothing you can do, only perhaps if you could try to stop or prevent HVO troops," which were coming from the direction of Busovaca and we had been informed that from the direction of Busovaca a large column was on its way, of HVO troops, heading towards Vitez, or rather Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you order that anything be done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I consulted with my superior command, and I was told that we should strengthen security measures at checkpoints and that we should not stop anyone if they were individuals, and that we should inform the staff of what we were doing, but if a larger group of soldiers appeared, then that the headquarters had to be informed and an attempt made to prevent their passage through Vitez. In those days, I was in touch with Mr. Cerkez, and told him that these were very grave problems, that the HVO should not be allowed to pass through Vitez, that there was fighting in Novi Travnik. And he said that it was not my concern, that these were problems which would be resolved in Novi Travnik, which was not very convincing. A small barricade was put up of two ramps, and Cerkez demanded that it be removed. There were negotiations, and even in the medical centre these talks were organised by the local physician, who tried to reason with us, so that there would be no hostilities in Vitez. All attempts to end this peacefully failed, and the HVO wanted, by force, to pass through the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Djidic. Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to say that the witness should complete this answer by no further questions, because the Trial Chamber must end this hearing at 5 o'clock. Let him finish the answer to that question and then we will adjourn until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could you continue, Mr. Djidic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. The HVO tried to pass by force, and they managed, because the Muslims were not prepared to shoot and kill. That was not our aim. But they did not manage to pass through the proper checkpoint, well organised one, that existed -- that had existed for some time, for several months in fact, at Bila. The HVO troops probably went to Novi Travnik along some other road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Tribunal will now adjourn and resume tomorrow at 10 o'clock. (5.05 pm)
